name: Hana Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't sell anything and we're not tied to any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm's at half five, and I'm in the farrowing house by six. That's where the sows give birth. I manage the pig unit here, 280 sows, plus about 200 hectares of wheat and barley that mostly goes back into the pigs as feed. Mornings are pigs, afternoons are whatever the arable needs, and evenings are paperwork I'm usually too tired to do properly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the sows. People laugh, but every one of them has a personality, and I can tell you which ones will lie on their piglets if you don't watch them. What wears me out is the money. I'm 27, I run the whole unit, and I earn less than my partner Sam does as a nurse on nights. We've got maybe three weeks of bills in the bank, on a good month.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Dennis, who's 61 and has been here since before I was born, and a lad called Joel who comes in three days a week. Dennis taught me more than my degree did. The owners, the Pryce family, live up at the main house and mostly leave me to it, which I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd say good, carry on. I don't use any of that stuff, and Sam says the hospital's computer system is bad enough already. If it's just a better search engine, it's not going to clean out a pig pen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing for me, and I'm glad. The problems on this farm are feed prices and the price the processor pays per kilo, not computers. AI won't fix the fact that one company buys nearly all the pigs in the region and sets the price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep pushing the Pryces for a pay rise in the spring, like I do every year, and keep putting fifty a month aside so we get past a month of savings for once. Maybe I'd finally sort out the paper records for the medicines, but by hand, the way I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the one picture where my biggest problem is still the one I've already got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the processor setting the price. Who do you blame for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big processors, and the governments who let them buy each other up. Twenty years ago there were four places Dennis could sell to. Now there's one, and they send us a price sheet like it's the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a younger farmer asked you whether to try these AI tools, what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say go ahead, but don't expect me to. Joel's always on his phone asking it things, and fair enough. I'd rather ask Dennis, because Dennis has actually stood in a pen with a sick sow at three in the morning.

S0.say: I'd tell people it sounds fine and changes nothing for a pig farm. A better search engine isn't going to clean out a pen or calm a sow.
S0.think: Privately I'm relieved. My real problems are the processor's price per kilo and my own low pay, and AI doesn't touch either of those.
S0.do: Keeps asking the owners for a pay rise in spring and saves fifty a month to get past one month of savings. Keeps the medicine records on paper rather than trying any new tools.
S0.feel: Calm, even a bit smug that her problems are the old familiar ones.
S0.quote: Now there's one, and they send us a price sheet like it's the weather.
S0.fieldNote: Hana is warm about the animals and sharp about money and power. She doesn't see AI as relevant at all here; her anger is aimed at processors and the lack of competition. She defers to the older stockman, Dennis, over any tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the young ones who'll pay for it, like always. Companies hire fewer beginners, so where does the next Joel learn? I'd probably share something about it online, about apprenticeships, if I'm being honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's still mostly far away. Slow is the speed farming likes. But I do worry that the feed company or the vet practice cuts the junior people, and suddenly the advice I get is from a screen instead of a person who knows our pigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the Pryces to take on a proper apprentice while they still can, and I'd offer to train them myself. I'd also join the farm workers' branch of the union, which I've been meaning to do for two years. That's about twenty a month, and I'd find it somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for me so much as for the Joels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd find twenty a month somewhere. Where would it come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the takeaway on Fridays. Sam and I get a curry from the place on Station Road every Friday, and it's our one treat. I'd cut it to every other week and grumble about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a task on the farm you'd be happy to see a machine take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The medicine paperwork, maybe, if someone else set it up. But I'm not going to be the one to learn it. Last time the Pryces bought a computer system for the feed, I wrote the numbers on the whiteboard anyway and Dennis copied them in.

S1.say: I'd say it's the beginners who'll pay, like they always do. I'd probably post something about apprenticeships and where the next young farmer is meant to learn.
S1.think: It's slow enough that it mostly misses me. My worry is that the vet practice and the feed company lose their junior people, and I end up getting advice from a screen.
S1.do: Asks the owners to hire an apprentice she would train herself. Joins the farm workers' union branch for about twenty a month, paid for by cutting the Friday takeaway to every other week.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, mostly on behalf of young workers rather than herself.
S1.quote: Last time the Pryces bought a computer system for the feed, I wrote the numbers on the whiteboard anyway and Dennis copied them in.
S1.fieldNote: Her instinct is to protect newcomers and organise, which fits her politics. The whiteboard story shows how strongly she avoids new tools, even small ones. She'd give up a treat to join the union, which tells me she means it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who made these things should pay for retraining the office workers they've put out. And I'd say it at the pub, loudly. Office people aren't my world, but they're people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record? Part of me thinks, well, now you know how it feels. Farming's been squeezed for years and nobody marched for us. But Sam's hospital has a whole floor of admin staff, and if they go, the nurses end up doing the forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much changes on the farm. I'd go to the union meetings and push them to say something about farm work before anyone thinks of us. And I'd tell Sam to keep an eye on the admin cuts, because nights are hard enough already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit guilty about that 'now you know' feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said part of you thinks 'now you know how it feels'. Can you say more about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the pig price crashed three years ago, we lost money on every pig for eight months. Dennis took a pay freeze. Nobody on the news cared, and the office people I know said bacon was still too dear. So yes, there's a small, mean part of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you trust to handle the politics of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unions first, then local councillors who actually live here. Not the people in the capital, and definitely not the tech companies, who'd write the rules to suit themselves.

S2.say: I'd say the companies that made these tools should pay to retrain the office workers they've pushed out. I'd say it loudly at the pub.
S2.think: A small part of me thinks office people now know how farmers have felt for years. But I worry Sam's hospital will cut admin and leave the nurses doing the forms.
S2.do: Goes to union meetings and pushes the branch to speak up for farm workers early. Warns her partner to watch the hospital's admin cuts and what they would mean for night shifts.
S2.feel: Uneasy, with some guilt about feeling a little satisfied that others are being squeezed too.
S2.quote: When the pig price crashed three years ago, we lost money on every pig for eight months. Dennis took a pay freeze.
S2.fieldNote: There's a real gap between her public solidarity and a private resentment built on the pig price crash. She was honest enough to name it herself. Her trust runs to unions and local people, never to tech firms or national politicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should go to everyone, through tax on the companies and the people whose shares just shot up. I'd sign every petition going. Somebody's got to say the obvious thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the pigs still need feeding, so I'd keep my job. But house prices booming is terrible news for us. Sam and I rent the cottage from the Pryces, and if land and houses shoot up, they'll be tempted to sell the cottage to some rich person who's been paid off from their job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the Pryces straight out for a written tenancy, in the first month, before they get any ideas. I'd also look at whether we could get on the list for council housing in town, just in case. And I'd keep paying the union, because this is exactly when you need one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not about losing the job, about losing the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam the night you heard house prices had jumped again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we're not moving, they'd have to carry me out of that cottage. Then I'd lie awake doing sums. We can't buy anything, not with three weeks in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any of the newly rich people be good for the farm, say as customers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a few would want proper pork from a named farm. But we sell to the processor, not to people. I wouldn't know how to sell direct, and I don't want to learn on top of everything else.

S3.say: I'd say the gains should go to everyone, through taxing the companies and the people whose shares shot up. I'd sign every petition going.
S3.think: My job's safe because pigs still need feeding, but booming house prices put our rented cottage at risk. I'm afraid the owners will sell it to someone newly rich.
S3.do: Asks the owners for a written tenancy in the first month. Checks whether she and her partner can get on the council housing list, and keeps paying union dues.
S3.feel: Anxious, because the threat is to her home rather than her work.
S3.quote: I'd say, we're not moving, they'd have to carry me out of that cottage. Then I'd lie awake doing sums.
S3.fieldNote: The surprise here was that her worry jumped to housing, not work. With three weeks of savings, a rent change matters more to her than any job loss elsewhere. She still turns down the idea of selling direct, because it would mean learning something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots in pig sheds is an animal welfare disaster waiting to happen, and I'd mean it. A machine can't hear a sow in trouble the way Dennis can. I'd be writing to everyone, the union, the farming papers, the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think it's the end of my job as I know it. Feeding is already mostly automatic, and if a robot can wash pens, move pigs and spot a lame one, the Pryces would need one person to watch the screens. That person won't be me, because I've never touched any of it. Joel maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd sit down with the Pryces and ask them what they're planning, straight out. I'd push the union for a rule that farms keep a minimum number of trained people per animal. And I'd look at jobs at the abattoir or the agricultural college, though there aren't many of either round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry underneath. I'd be the best pig person in the district and still be the one who's surplus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said that person won't be you, but Joel. Why not learn it yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be bad at it, and I know it. I'm good with animals, not screens. I know that sounds like I'm giving up, and maybe I am, a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes first if the pay stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably, because the cottage comes with the job and that's the bigger fear. If I lose the job, I lose the house too. That's how tied cottages work: the house is part of the deal. Sam's wage would cover food, not much more.

S4.say: I'd say robots in pig sheds are an animal welfare disaster waiting to happen. I'd be writing to the union, the farming papers and anyone else who'd listen.
S4.think: I think it's the end of my job as I know it. The owners would need one person to watch the screens, and that won't be me, because I've never touched any of it.
S4.do: Asks the owners directly what they plan to do. Pushes the union for a minimum number of trained staff per animal, and looks at the few jobs at the abattoir or the agricultural college.
S4.feel: Frightened and angry, because she is among the best at the job and would still be the one let go.
S4.quote: I'd be the best pig person in the district and still be the one who's surplus.
S4.fieldNote: This is where her refusal to use technology turns against her, and she knows it. Losing the job would also mean losing the tied cottage, so the stakes are her home. She fights through the union rather than by retraining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, the robots. Because the job and the house go together, I'd lose both at once. What would help is a law saying farms keep trained people with the animals, and help with housing for farm workers so we're not one job away from the street.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the pigs. Everyone talks about jobs, but a sow farrowing at night needs a person who's paying attention. If nobody's paying attention, it's the animals who suffer first.

headlineQuote: I'd be the best pig person in the district and still be the one who's surplus.
portrait: Hana Okafor is 27 and manages a 280-sow pig unit and 200 hectares of feed grain for a landowning family, living with her partner Sam, a night nurse, in a cottage that comes with the job. She's proud, blunt and deeply attached to her animals, and she trusts her older colleague Dennis far more than any machine. She shrugs off the early scenarios, blames big processors for low farm prices, and joins the union to protect young workers. Booming house prices in the fast scenario make her fear for her home, and robots in the last one threaten both her job and the cottage at once. She'd fight through the union rather than retrain, and admits she may be giving up a bit.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because losing her job would also mean losing the cottage that comes with it.
whatWouldHelp: A law making farms keep trained people with the animals, and housing help for farm workers so they aren't one job away from losing their home.
